live_web_research.page_text: [2610.10862] A mesh-based neural energy method for the simulation of heterogeneous composites Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science arXiv:2610.10862 (cs) [Submitted on 7 Oct 2026] Title: A mesh-based neural energy method for the simulation of heterogeneous composites Authors: Pius J. M. Wichmann , Stefan Hildebrand , Sandra Klinge View a PDF of the paper titled A mesh-based neural energy method for the simulation of heterogeneous composites, by Pius J. M. Wichmann and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Modeling heterogeneous materials remains a challenge for physics-informed neural networks such as the deep energy method (DEM). The DEM and its variants, here collectively referred to as the neural energy method (NEM), offer a differentiable variational framework. However, their conventional collocation-based implementation (C-NEM) often suffers from physically inadmissible displacement oscillations, integration errors, and high computational costs from automatic differentiation. This work introduces the mesh-based neural energy method (M-NEM), extending the NEM through a mesh-based discretization of the displacement field. By interpolating nodal displacements via shape functions, the M-NEM imposes a kinematic constraint that suppresses oscillations. Furthermore, the method replaces automatic differentiation with algebraic shape function derivatives for strain computation and employs high-order Gaussian quadrature for accurate energy integration. On a directly comparable benchmark problem, the M-NEM reduces stress errors by up to three orders of magnitude relative to the C-NEM while being one to two orders of magnitude faster. On two further benchmarks involving extreme stiffness contrasts, only the M-NEM converges. A comparative study of neural architectures reveals that radial basis function neural networks (RBFNNs) yield optimal performance within the M-NEM, resolving sharp gradients at material interfaces with higher accuracy than multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with random Fourier feature (RFF) mapping and faster convergence than Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs). live_web_research.page_text: Ruger Suspends Production of a Range of Prominent Gun Models - Shooting News Weekly --> --> Skip to content Ruger Suspends Production of a Range of Prominent Gun Models By Jim Shepherd • October 14, 2026 • 10 Comments • 3 minutes of reading • Business , Gun News Ruger Precision Rifle (image: Cerakote ) Yesterday, distributors got a memo from Ruger telling them that, in keeping with their Ruger 2030 product portfolio review, they had made the decision to suspend several “lower-volume and legacy product families.” Those suspensions include the “immediate” suspension of the Ruger LCR, Ruger SP101, GP100 and Bearcat handguns. According to the memo, all open distributor orders for these guns would be cancelled. Those immediate suspensions were only the tip of the iceberg. Other current-generation suspended product families will continue through final planned production runs over the remainder of 2026: SR1911, LC Carbine, PC Charger, PC Carbine, LC Charger, Redhawk, Super Redhawk, Blackhawk, Super Blackhawk, Single-Series revolvers, Vaquero, No. 1, 77-Series rifles, Hawkeye and the Ruger Precision Rifle. Ruger Vaquero These products, the memo reads, will be placed on allocation. Open orders that haven’t been filled by the end of production will be cancelled. What’s not been widely distributed with these notices is the fact Ruger isn’t dumping these lines. They’ve paused lines before. Some, like the Ruger Precision Rifle were paused to allow for improvements. Others, like the Red Label shotgun, were paused for years before being reintroduced. Speaking with Ruger officials, I was reminded — repeatedly — that they realized the importance of many of these products with distributors, retailers and consumers. That’s why they emphasized the moves should be viewed as a company responsibly managing the products’ evolution, not simply ending their history. Ruger PC Carbine Suspending production, they assure me, didn’t necessarily mean saying goodbye to the product families. In fact, they believe opportunities exist to bring legacy platforms forward via new designs, modern manufacturing, and “meaningful innovation.” “Just as importantly,” the distributor memo reads, “they do not change who Ruger is, the markets in which we compete or the consumers we are committed to serving. Our heritage remains an important part of our future. Our responsibility is to build upon that heritage by ensuring the products that carry the Ruger name continue to evolve with the needs and expectations of today’s consumers.” The notification included several FAQs that appear to be reassurances that Ruger isn’t moving away from their revolvers, traditional rifles or legacy lines. In fact, it reads “These decisions should not be interpreted as Ruger moving away from the markets, product categories or consumers we have historically served. They reflect decisions about specific current-generation products and how we best allocate resources today while evaluating opportunities for future products.” During NASGW, distributors were surprised to get notification that a number of Ruger product “families,” including the GP 100 revolver were being “paused” as part of the Ruger’s 2030 product portfolio review. Some, like the GP 100 were being paused immediately. Others will continue until 2026 production ends. And, yes, they write, they believe opportunities exist to bring a number of these “important Ruger product platforms back to market in new forms from updated designs and new features to improved manufacturing and broader generational changes.” Several of the guns that will be part of the “pause” certainly hold key places in Ruger’s history, from the SR1911 to the truly iconic revolvers and Hawkeye rifles. But the determining factor in manufacturing isn’t product recognition, it’s product sales. Ruger SR1911 While I’m not privy to Ruger’s sales numbers, I’m reasonably confident that the sales of all the products slated for suspension represent less than five percent of the company’s current sales volume. That’s not a slam on any of them, it’s simply a reflection of the changing tastes of consumers and the fact that many legacy products can find themselves more significant in a historical perspective than in the current commercial marketplace. of Several Major Models Share Post Donate Menu Search Search Ruger Suspends Production of Several Major Models by Evan Brune, Executive Editor posted on October 14, 2026 News Support NRA American Rifleman DONATE ** When you buy products through the links on our site, we may earn a commission that supports NRA's mission to protect, preserve and defend the Second Amendment. ** Ruger announced a major change to several of its longtime product lines this week, stating that it would immediately suspend production of several models while finishing out current production runs of other models through 2026. "Ruger announced changes to several current-generation product families yesterday as part of our ongoing Ruger 2030 strategy," said Abbey Clary, Ruger's director of media, advertising and public relations. "This does not necessarily mean these product families are permanently discontinued." Effective immediately, Ruger is ceasing production of its LCR, SP101, GP100 and Bearcat revolvers. The company plans to complete its final production runs of the following models for 2026: SR1911, LC Carbine, PC Charger, PC Carbine, LC Charger, Redhawk, Super Redhawk, Blackhawk, Super Blackhawk, Single-Series revolvers, Vaquero, No. 1, 77-Series rifles, Hawkeye and Ruger Precision Rifle. "We recognize how important these platforms are to Ruger’s heritage and to our customers," Clary said. "In many cases, we see opportunities to bring them forward through new designs, improved features and modern manufacturing methods. We expect some of these names and product families to return in new forms in the future, but do not have specific product plans or reintroduction timelines at this time." With this shift, Ruger's handgun product lines continuing into 2027 will consist of the company's LCP offerings, RXM, MAX-9, Security-380, Security-9, Ruger 5.7, Mark IV and 22 Charger. In its revolver line, Ruger will continue making its affordable Wrangler and Super Wrangler models. For rifles, remaining Ruger offerings will consist of the company's American Rifle and American Rimfire line, as well as the Ruger Precision Rimfire, Harrier, 10/22 and Mini-14 models. "These decisions reflect our review of consumer demand, evolving market preferences, manufacturing complexity and the long-term profitability of each product family," Clary said. "The goal is to focus our resources on the products consumers want most today while creating capacity for future product development and manufacturing modernization." article.body:
Mesh-based neural method improves composite simulations, not production capacity

The paper introduces a mesh-based neural energy method (M-NEM) for simulating heterogeneous composites. It interpolates nodal displacements with shape functions, replacing automatic differentiation with algebraic shape-function derivatives and using high-order Gaussian quadrature for energy integration.

On a directly comparable benchmark, the authors report stress errors up to three orders of magnitude lower and computation one to two orders of magnitude faster than the collocation-based method. On two further benchmarks with extreme stiffness contrasts, only M-NEM converged.

This is a simulation method, not a factory or production-line change. The paper specifies no industrial deployment, output capacity, physical production constraint, customer or supply-chain effect.
